findings.message: The feedback of the second wrong option ends with 'The / sign keeps the fraction, and % gives the leftover, not the count of times', which is the correct statement almost word for word. The third option's feedback also confirms that the first half is right and says what % gives. The learner gets the answer in the feedback, so the second attempt tests nothing.
The feedback of the wrong option 'undefined' says 'Line 2 stored null, which is a value you choose.' This names the correct answer outright, so the learner's second attempt is no longer a prediction.

The feedback of the wrong option 'false' ends with 'here the number 0', which names the correct answer outright. The feedback of the wrong option '15' also states the full rule ('gives back the left side when it is falsy, and 0 is falsy'), which leaves only 0 as the answer. The learner's second attempt is no longer a prediction.

Hint 3 ('Put full inside the if block and low inside the else block') states the whole structure of the solution. Only the trivial placement of the braces is left, so the hint no longer stays near the solution without stating it.

The option 'The last return wins, so aisle comes back' is tagged no-return-last-value (a function with no return gives back its last computed value). Its belief is that a later return replaces an earlier one, which the unit file lists under code-after-return-runs, so the tag is wrong and would route remediation to the wrong misconception.

The option '3' (the sum of the ids) is tagged object-has-position, which is the belief that object values are read by position. Adding cabin.id instead of cabin.beds is a different slip (reading the wrong key), so the tag would route remediation to the wrong misconception.
Hint 2 ('map returns a new array and does not edit the original') is word for word the correct option, so the learner is handed the answer at the concept level.
Hint 2 ('filter keeps an element when the callback result is truthy') repeats the correct option nearly verbatim, so it states the answer instead of naming the concept.
Feedback of option '12 null' says 'When nothing matches it returns undefined', which gives away the second half of the correct answer and removes the learner's second attempt.
Feedback of option 'some gives null and filter gives an empty array' says 'some returns a boolean, so it gives false', which states the first half of the correct option and reveals the answer.
Hint 2 ('The ... in a parameter list collects arguments into an array') restates the correct option almost word for word, so it states the answer instead of only naming the concept.
Hint 2 ('=== on objects compares where they live, not what they hold') is the correct option rephrased, so the learner is handed the answer at the concept level.
Hint 2 ('Hoisting moves the declaration, not the assignment') is the correct option restated, so it gives the answer instead of only naming the concept.

Hint 2 ('A new call of the outer function creates new variables') restates the correct option ('Each makeJar call creates its own coins') almost word for word, so it hands over the answer instead of only naming the concept.

Hint 3 says each call drop(2) adds 2 to the starting coins. Read literally, both calls add 2 to the starting value 3, which points to 5 for the second call (the wrong option). The second call must add 2 to the value the first call left behind (5), so the hint points the wrong way.

The reference points to Promise.prototype.finally(), but the snippet uses the try...catch...finally statement inside an async function. A learner who follows the link reads about a different construct; the try...catch page (as used by the sibling item) fits the code.

Hint 1 already states the key rule (listeners fire in registration order, not definition order). Hint 1 should only point at where to look; the rule belongs in hint 2, so the hints do not rise in strength.

dom-and-events.lesson-4: The card says closest(selector) returns the nearest ancestor that matches. closest also tests the element itself first, so a click whose target is the matching element returns that element. A learner delegating on clicks of the item itself would be misled by the word ancestor.

Hint 3 says both plain say calls come before the callback in the printed order. That states the full output order ('doors open', 'seats filled', then 'curtain'), so only one option remains and the learner has nothing left to work out. It should narrow the choice, not state it.

The correct-option feedback and the explanation both say 'bike has no own go' and 'bike finds the same function', but the snippet has no variable named bike; the instance is called b. A learner looking for bike in the code is confused.

Hint 2 says a single unnamed value is 'found by position, as the only one'. A default export is not found by position; it is stored under the fixed name default and the importer simply binds it to a name of its choice. The hint teaches a wrong mechanism.

Hint 1 says to compare 'the ids on line 7 with the ids on line 5', but line 5 (return { count };) contains no ids; ids is declared on line 4. A learner looks for ids on line 5, finds nothing, and may be sent the wrong way. It should point at the returned object on line 5 rather than at an ids on it.
The feedback of option 'tidy\ndone' ends with 'so line 5 throws', which states the correct outcome (the TypeError) and so reveals the answer; the learner has no second attempt left to reason out.

'Return running names by first start' can be read as order of the first start ever, or order of the current run. For ['start a','start b','stop a','start a'] the Set reference returns ['b','a'] (the restarted name moves to the end), while the literal reading 'by first start' gives ['a','b']. No test pins this down, and hint 3 and the explanation repeat the 'order of first start' wording, so a careful learner who keeps first-start order is marked wrong by a hidden choice.

The feedback of '6 6' states 'It never visits the stops after the 3', and the feedback of '3 6' states that 'it is find that quits early'. Both give away the mechanism and the visited count of the correct answer ('6 3') instead of only addressing the mistaken belief.

The feedback of the option that says === compares the sign of zero begins 'It is the other way round. === says they are equal, and Object.is is the one that separates them.' That states the correct answer outright instead of addressing the mistaken belief, so the learner gets no real second attempt.
The feedback of '4\nundefined' ends with 'it answers 0 there', which states the second printed value of the correct answer outright. It should only say that the trap also runs for a missing key.

The feedback of 'then' and 'finally' says 'nothing is printed'. In both cases the rejection reaches the end of the chain unhandled, and under the execution model that prints 'Uncaught (in promise) TypeError' (and a real console reports it too). Only console.log(log) prints nothing, so the learner is told something the program does not do.

The snippet uses the compound assignment `+=` (total += crate), which no earlier unit or declared prerequisite teaches; Variables and Loops only show `x = x + n`. A beginner meets an unexplained operator inside a trace item.

The loop body uses `song += ...`, the compound assignment `+=`, which neither this unit's declared prerequisites nor any earlier unit teaches (they use `x = x + n`). It is needed to read the program being ordered.

Rated 3, but it is a three-line snippet with one blank and three chips (var, let, const) and one idea; the other single-idea fill in the unit (block-scope.fill-01) is 2. It should be 2 so difficulty rises inside the lesson.

The task (average of an array, 0 when empty) is a plain loop-accumulator exercise; any correct answer is written in the natural order and never touches the temporal dead zone. Only one wrong solution hits it, so the item does not test this lesson's concept.

Rated 4, but it is the simplest await case (one await, one plain line after the call) and opens the lesson. The Parsons item parsons-01 in the same lesson has the same program shape and is rated 3, so the lesson does not rise and the two ratings contradict each other. This predict item should be 3.

The lesson concept is that a class is syntax over prototypes. This task exercises only extends and super.cost(), which is the declared prerequisite class-inheritance. Nothing in the task, tests, hints or explanation touches the prototype link, a prototype method or the constructor function, so the item does not test the lesson's own concept.

Hint 2 and the first wrong option's feedback say a WeakMap key may also be 'a non-registered symbol'. Symbols, and the registered versus non-registered distinction, are taught only in lesson 4 of this unit, and this lesson's declared prerequisites do not include them. A learner in lesson 3 meets an unexplained idea in the feedback. The item can be solved without it, so only the hint and feedback wording needs to drop the parenthetical.

Rated 4, but it orders five lines whose only constraints are that the two declarations come first and add comes before the true check. The second hint already gives the whole structure, and there is no subtle effect to trace. The Parsons items of comparable size in the other advanced units are rated 3. This is a 3 for the advanced track.

Rated 4, but the learner only has to pick the one chip that removes the entry from the array (pop). The reachability idea was already needed for the lesson's rated-3 concept item, and the chips are plain array methods. This is the same level as that item, so it is a 3 for the advanced track.

Rated 5, but it is a one-step fix: valueOf returns a string, so change it to return the number. The lesson's predict item (valueOf versus toString by hint) is rated 4 and needs more steps, so the fix item is easier than the item before it and does not belong at the top of the track's scale. It is a 4.

Rated 5 and placed first in its lesson, but it is one trace of throw, try, finally and catch over two frames, which is Errors-unit material at the same depth as the lesson's other items rated 4. Opening the lesson at the top of the scale leaves no room to rise within the lesson. It is a 4.

The lesson concept is following a failure through several functions. This item is a plain promise rejection and recovery chain (Promise.reject, then, catch) with no function calling another, so it re-tests promise-rejection-flow from the Promises unit instead of the lesson's concept. It has the same shape as promise-rejection-flow.fill-01 in the advanced track, where it is rated 3, and here it is rated 4.

Below the Expert track. It only asks the learner to call a function passed as an argument and add 3, which is Functions-unit material (intermediate level) with two lines of arithmetic. Expert items are rated 4 to 5 and expect several combined ideas; this has one.

Below the Expert track. The whole fix is dot access versus bracket access with a variable key (fare.m versus fare[m]), a basic Objects-unit idea. The strategy table around it adds nothing the learner has to reason about, so it does not reach the 4 to 5 range.

Below the Expert track. The bug is that the function ignores its send parameter and calls mail directly, so the fix is to call the parameter. That is a one-step Functions-unit idea with a single changed token; it is not a 4 to 5 item for expert learners.

Below the Expert track. Both blanks are solved by passing functions by name instead of calling them, and the two chips that call or hard-code a value fail for the same simple reason. This is intermediate callback usage, not an expert-level combination of ideas.
